points: Real growth: (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1 = 1.30 ÷ 1.332 − 1 ≈ −2.4%. Volume fell.

The board was celebrating a business that shrank. Report real, naira and dollar figures side by side.
Targets and bonuses set in nominal naira reward inflation, not performance.

points: Until 2023 the CBN held an official rate; the bureau-de-change rate shows the market's price. The gap peaked at 71% (May 2016).
A premium signals rationing — Principle 6 at work — and an incentive to arbitrage (Principle 4).
June 2023 unification: the naira moved from about ₦460 to ₦750/$ within weeks, then past ₦1,500.
Today: ₦1,347/$ (CBN, 4 Nov 2026). Use the rate you actually transact at.

figures.title: Did Savers Beat Inflation? The Real Policy Rate
points: Real rate = (1 + policy rate) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1 — the same arithmetic as real revenue.
For most of 2016–2024 it was negative, falling below −8% in 2024: naira savings lost value, pushing savers into dollars, land and stock.
Today: MPR 23%, inflation 14.6% → real rate +7.3%. Holding naira now pays.
Part of the jump in January 2025 is the new CPI — measurement, not just policy.

figures.title: Oil Earns Nigeria's Dollars — Yet Reserves Don't Simply Track It
points: The causal channel is clear: oil and gas earn most of the FX (Trap 3).
Yet the correlation is only 0.54 in the same month — and 0.17 a year later.
Why? Oil-backed loans and forward sales, CBN intervention, Eurobond and loan inflows, and 2026's reserve build despite a volatile oil price.
A causal link can hide inside a weak correlation, and a strong correlation can hide no link at all.

concepts.title: Seeing the Economy Before GDP Is Published
concepts.plain: GDP for a quarter arrives about two months after it ends. Nowcasting estimates what is happening now from faster signals: business surveys (PMI), payments, fuel and power use, port traffic — and your own orders.
concepts.formula: PMI > 50 expanding · < 50 contracting
concepts.example: The Stanbic IBTC PMI was 55.7 in October 2026 (56.4 in September): a ninth month of growth, but input prices hit a four-month high on fuel costs — an early warning for margins.
concepts.why: Your own data are nowcasting signals: daily sales, distributor orders, collections and stock levels often tell you about the economy weeks before NBS does. Combine them with the PMI and the price data on one page.

checks.q: Your CFO wants to run the night shift because 'it lowers our average cost per carton'. Which reply best applies today's principles?
options: Agree — a lower average cost means each carton is now more profitable
Reject it — fixed costs make night shifts unprofitable in Nigeria
Ask whether the shift's extra revenue covers its extra cost, ignoring fixed costs we pay anyway
Postpone until next quarter's GDP data show whether demand is growing
checks.explain: C. Marginal thinking: only costs that change with the decision matter. A lower average cost can coexist with a loss on the extra output (−₦0.7m a night in our example). A confuses average with marginal; B blames the fixed costs, which are irrelevant to the decision; D waits for slow data on a question your own numbers answer.

checks.q: A director says: 'Inflation fell from 34.8% in December 2024 to 24.5% in January 2025 — down 10% in a month. We can cut prices.' What is the best response?
options: The fall partly reflects the new CPI base and basket; January has since been revised to 27.6%, and it is a 10-point fall, not 10% — compare like with like before repricing
He is right: a 10-point fall in one month is strong evidence that price pressures have ended
He is right on the direction but wrong on size: it fell about 30%, so cut prices even more
Ignore inflation data altogether; watch only the exchange rate
checks.explain: A. Three corrections in one: a rebasing break, a later revision, and points vs percent. B ignores the measurement break; C computes the percent change correctly (−30%) but draws the wrong conclusion from a broken comparison; D throws away useful information.

checks.q: Which pair of signals would best tell an FMCG board, **this month**, that demand is weakening?
options: Last quarter's GDP release and the IMF's annual forecast
The CPI base year and the GDP base year
The 10-year bond yield and the oil price
The PMI new-orders index and the firm's own distributor orders and collections
checks.explain: D. Fast, demand-side signals: the PMI arrives within days and the firm's own orders and collections are real-time. A is slow; B is about measurement, not demand; C matters for financing and FX, not this month's demand.

In a Nigerian boardroom
Where

flow.title: What Did ₦1bn of Idle Cash Really Cost in 2024?

head: ₦1bn, end-2023 → end-2024
Naira, end-2024
Real (Dec-23 ₦)
rows: Leave it in a current account (0%)

steps: Inflation in the year to Dec 2024 was **34.8%**: ₦1 at end-2024 bought what ₦0.74 bought a year earlier (1 ÷ 1.348).
Idle cash therefore **lost about ₦258m** of purchasing power — a real cost that no invoice ever shows.
A one-year T-bill bought in **January 2024** yielded about **11.5%**; yields near 20% came only after the February–March hikes. Real return: 1.115 ÷ 1.348 − 1 ≈ **−17%**.
Pre-buying hedged the naira's fall from **₦899 to ₦1,535/$** (+71%) — but tied up cash and warehouse space, and stock can spoil. That is **its** opportunity cost.
flow.aside: In 2024 the 'safe' choice — idle naira — was the most expensive one, and even T-bills lost in real terms. Only the **dollar-linked** option kept its value. With the real policy rate now about **+7%** (Part 2), that ranking has reversed.
flow.result: The cost of a decision is the **best alternative given up** — measured in real terms, not just in naira.
flow.notes:
Sources: NBS CPI Dec 2024 = 34.80% y/y (CBN statistics). 364-day NTB auction yields: 8.40% (10 Jan 2024), 11.54% (24 Jan 2024) — Nairametrics, 26 Jan 2024; 19% (late Feb) and 21.49% (6 Mar 2024) — Nairametrics/ThisDay. CBN official central rate: ₦899.39/$ (29 Dec 2023), ₦1,535.32/$ (31 Dec 2024) → ×1.707; real 1.707 ÷ 1.348 = 1.27.

Hindsight point: a treasurer who waited until March got 21% — still roughly −10% real measured against 2024 inflation (1.21 ÷ 1.348 − 1). (A bill bought on 24 January matures in January 2025; close enough for the lesson.) Ask: what would you do with ₦1bn today, when the real rate is positive?

flow.title: Should the Factory Run a Third (Night) Shift?

head: Per night of the third shift
₦ million
rows: Diesel — the grid is unreliable at night

steps: Finance says: 'average cost per carton falls from ₦5,000 to ₦4,900 because fixed costs are spread' — **true but irrelevant**.
Fixed costs (rent, depreciation, head office) are paid whether or not the shift runs. They are **not marginal**.
Ask only: does the **extra** revenue exceed the **extra** cost? Here it falls short by ₦0.7m a night.
The decision flips if diesel falls, the grid improves or the price rises — so those are the numbers to watch.
flow.aside: Find the break-even. At what diesel cost does the shift pay? (₦5.8m a night.) At what net price per carton? (₦4,617.) Good managers know the **two or three numbers that flip the decision**.
flow.result: Decide at the **margin**: compare extra benefit with extra cost. Averages and sunk costs mislead.
flow.notes: Illustrative figures. Day and evening shifts make 17,000 cartons at ₦85m a night (average ₦5,000); adding 6,000 cartons at ₦27.7m gives ₦112.7m ÷ 23,000 = ₦4,900. Break-evens: diesel 27.0 − 18.0 − 3.2 = 5.8; price (18.0 + 3.2 + 6.5) / 6,000 = ₦4,617. Sunk-cost example to add verbally: an ERP licence already paid for should not decide whether to keep using the system. Links to Session 2 (pricing) and Session 4 (cost structure).

flow.title: People Respond to Incentives — Often Unexpectedly

cards.title: Petrol subsidy
cards.body: Pump price held near **₦185/litre** until May 2023 while neighbours paid far more. Result: cross-border smuggling and a subsidy bill above **₦4trn** in 2022.
cards.foot: Incentives change behaviour at the margin.

cards.title: Multiple exchange rates
cards.body: In May 2016 the street rate was **71% above** the official rate. Anyone with official access could buy cheap and sell dear; **round-tripping** grew while genuine importers queued.
cards.foot: A price gap is an incentive.

cards.title: FX restrictions on imports
cards.body: Barring 41 items from the official FX window (2015) aimed to boost local production. It also **raised prices and rewarded smuggling** through porous borders.
cards.foot: Watch what people do, not what the rule says.

flow.note: Before backing a policy — or a sales commission scheme — ask: **who gains, who loses, and how will each change behaviour?**
flow.notes: Sources: NNPC 'under-recovery' (petrol subsidy) ≈ ₦4.39trn in 2022; pump price ₦185/l before 29 May 2023. FX premium: CBN monthly averages, May 2016 — BDC vs official (see the exchange-rate chart in Part 2). CBN circular of June 2015 excluded 41 items from the official FX market. Company example to ask for: a commission plan that paid on volume and destroyed margin.

flow.kicker: PRINCIPLE 5 · TRADE CAN MAKE EVERYONE BETTER OFF
flow.title: Comparative Advantage: Why the 'Better' Producer Still Gains
steps: Nigeria is faster at **both** goods: it has the **absolute advantage** in each.
But a bag of cocoa costs Nigeria **2 tonnes** of cement forgone, and Ghana only **1 tonne**. Ghana has the **comparative advantage** in cocoa; Nigeria has it in cement.
If each leans towards what it gives up least to make, total output rises: the same 25 bags of cocoa plus **10 extra tonnes** of cement.
Trade at 1.5 t per bag: Ghana swaps 10 bags for 15 t and ends with **10 bags + 15 t** (was 10 + 10); Nigeria ends with **35 t + 15 bags** (was 30 + 15). **Both gain.**
flow.result: Gains from trade come from **comparative** advantage — differences in opportunity cost — not from being best at everything.
flow.notes: Mankiw ch. 3 ('Interdependence and the Gains from Trade') uses a farmer and a rancher; the logic is identical. Numbers are illustrative, not real productivities. Firm-level version: should your best salesperson also do the invoicing because she is faster at it? No — her opportunity cost is lost sales. Who loses from trade (import-competing workers and firms) is part of Session 12.

flow.title: Markets Usually Work — Governments Can Sometimes Help

left.title: 6 · Markets usually work well
items: A price summarises scarcity: when it rises, buyers economise and sellers supply more — with no one coordinating them.
When the official naira rate was held below the market, dollars **were rationed**: queues and a parallel market replaced the price signal.
Price controls create shortages, queues or black markets — the price is still paid, just in another form.
Adam Smith's 'invisible hand': self-interest, guided by prices, can serve the common good.

right.title: 7 · Governments can sometimes help
right.tag: When markets fail — and when the state has capacity
items: **Property rights and contracts**: markets work only if courts enforce them.
**Externalities**: pollution, gas flaring and congestion impose costs that prices ignore (Session 5).
**Market power**: a dominant firm or platform can price above the efficient level (Session 4).
'Sometimes' is the key word: policy can also fail — through poor design, weak capacity or capture.

flow.note: The manager's question is never 'market or state?' but **'what is failing here, and will the proposed fix work better than the failure?'**
flow.notes: Mankiw ch. 1, principles 6–7 and the invisible-hand passage. Use FX rationing (2015–2023) as the bridge: the control did not remove the cost of dollars; it moved it into queues, premiums and lost production.

flow.title: Living Standards Depend on What a Country Produces
points: **Real** output per person (constant 2015 US$) was **$2,584 in 2014**, near its 2015 peak, and **$2,325 in 2024**: about **10% lower**.
Population grew about **2–2.6% a year**; output barely kept up — echoing **1992–2002**, when the LBS case IB-90 reports GDP growth of 2.25% against population growth of 2.8% (older data).
The **current-dollar** line falls by two-thirds — mostly the **naira's collapse**, not lost production. It also jumps in 2019 where the rebased GDP series begins.
Wages rise sustainably only with **output per worker**: power, skills, technology, institutions (Session 7).
flow.notes:
Sources: World Bank WDI NY.GDP.PCAP.KD and NY.GDP.PCAP.CD (updated Oct 2026): 2014 $2,583.6 real (2015 peak $2,585.7) / $3,088.7 current; 2024 $2,324.6 / $1,084.2. SP.POP.GROW: 2.6% (2014) to 2.1% (2024). 'The Business Environment of Nigeria' (IB-90), p. 6, for 1992–2002.

This slide is also a data-literacy lesson: the same 'GDP per head' tells opposite stories in current and constant dollars.

flow.kicker: PRINCIPLES 9 & 10 · THE ECONOMY AS A WHOLE — PREVIEW
flow.title: Money, Prices and the Short-Run Trade-Off
flow.lead:
**9.** Prices rise when the government finances itself by creating money.

**10.** In the short run, lowering inflation usually costs output and jobs.
flow.leadFoot: Full treatment and Nigerian data in the appendix and in Part II.

points.t: _The Ascent of Money_ shows inflation moving wealth from savers and bondholders to debtors. Argentina pegged, slashed inflation — and still defaulted in 2001 because **fiscal** discipline never followed.

points.h: Nigeria: money financing, then the bill
points.t: CBN 'Ways & Means' lending to the government reached about **₦22.7trn** before being securitised in 2023. Inflation peaked at **34.8%** in December 2024.

The CBN raised its policy rate from **18.75% to 27.5%** during 2024, began cutting only in **September 2025** as inflation fell, and is now at **23%** (September 2026). Volumes and jobs feel tightening **before** prices do.
When the MPC tightens, plan for **slower demand and tighter working capital** over the next year; when it eases, the reverse.

flow.notes: Sources: Ferguson, The Ascent of Money (2008), Introduction and ch. 2. Ways & Means: Senate approved securitisation of ₦22.7trn on 3–4 May 2023 (ThisDay); a further ₦7.3trn was securitised later, taking the total near ₦30trn. MPR path: CBN money-market indicators (18.75% Dec 2023; 27.50% Nov 2024; 27.0% from 23 Sep 2025; 26.5% from Feb 2026; 23.00% from 22 Sep 2026). Inflation: CBN/NBS CPI. Unemployment-measurement caveat (33.3% → 4.1% after NBS's 2023 methodology change) is in the appendix.

A confuses average with marginal; B blames the fixed costs, which are irrelevant to the decision; D waits for slow data on a question your own numbers answer.

flow.title: Read the Numbers
flow.sub: How official statistics are built — and the traps that catch managers.
flow.question: Did our firm actually grow — and what is the economy really doing?

flow.kicker: EVERY STATISTIC HAS A SUPPLY CHAIN
flow.title: From Concept to Headline: Where Errors Creep In

steps.label: Concept
steps.desc: What do we want to know? e.g. the cost of living.

steps.label: Definition
steps.desc: Which basket, households, prices, base year?

steps.label: Collection
steps.desc: Surveys, admin and tax records. Is the informal sector covered?

steps.label: Aggregation
steps.desc: Weights and index formulas turn thousands of prices into one number.

steps.label: Release
steps.desc: Headline first, detail later. Lags matter.

steps.label: Revision
steps.desc: Rebasing and new data change history — even recent history.

flow.note: Piketty's warning applies to every board paper: without precise sources, methods and concepts, **you can see everything and its opposite.**
flow.notes: Piketty, Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014), Introduction, 'A Debate without Data?'. Each link maps onto a trap in this part: definition (rebasing), coverage (share of what?), aggregation (CPI weights), revision (the 2025 inflation revision).

flow.title: How the CPI Is Built — a Five-Step Worked Example
steps: **Fix the basket**: what a typical household buys (quantities held constant).
**Collect prices** for each item in each period.
**Cost the basket** each year at that year's prices.
**Inflation** = 112.1 ÷ 100 − 1 = **12.1%**, even though rice got cheaper.
flow.result: The CPI tracks a **fixed basket**. Your firm's own input basket may inflate much faster or slower.
flow.notes: Mankiw ch. 23 uses hot dogs and hamburgers; this is a Lagos basket with illustrative prices. Ask: what is your company's 'basket' of inputs and how did its cost change? That is your firm's own inflation rate. Biases of the CPI (substitution, new goods, quality) are in the appendix.

flow.title: Inflation: Food Led, Core Followed — Then the Yardstick Changed
points: Dec 2024: **34.8%** on the old CPI (2009 base, food **51.8%** of the basket).
Jan 2025: new CPI (**2024 = 100**, food weight **40%**). First published as **24.48%**…
…then **revised to 27.61%** when NBS reviewed its method in Dec 2025. Even 'latest data' changes.
Sep 2026: headline **14.6%**, food 19.6%, core 13.0% — a genuine fall, on the new yardstick.
**Never compare across a rebasing** without the statistics office's linked series.
flow.notes: Sources: CBN statistics (inflation API) reproducing NBS CPI; NBS rebasing (Feb 2025: base 2009 → 2024, food weight 51.8% → 40%, The Guardian); NBS methodology review, Dec 2025 (Jan 2025 revised 24.48% → 27.61%, Nairametrics, 16 Jan 2026). Ask: what would you tell a union negotiating wages off 'inflation has halved'?

flow.title: The Day Nigeria's Economy 'Grew' 35%

stats.label: 2024 nominal GDP, rebased
stats.desc: New base year **2019** (was 2010), published by NBS in July 2025.

stats.label: vs the old estimate
stats.desc: Same economy, better measurement: fintech, creative industries, telecoms and more informal activity captured.

stats.label: Extra naira in anyone's pocket
stats.desc: Rebasing changes the **level**. Ratios drop overnight: debt-to-GDP, tax-to-GDP, credit-to-GDP.

flow.note: Before comparing GDP ratios across years or countries, ask: **which base year?** A covenant of 'debt below 40% of GDP' can be met overnight by a rebasing.

flow.title: Oil Is 4% of GDP — and Still Most of Nigeria's Exports

data.name: Share
labels: Crude oil's share of export value
Oil and gas share of export value

flow.source: Q2 2026. Sources: NBS GDP report; NBS Foreign Trade in Goods (crude ₦12.91trn, other ₦14.11trn incl. non-oil ₦3.72trn, of ₦27.0trn).
points: Oil adds little **value added** in real GDP — it is capital-intensive and measured at constant prices.
But oil earns most of the **dollars**: crude alone was about 48% of exports; oil and gas about 86%.
So the oil price still drives the **naira, reserves and government revenue**.
Always ask: share of **GDP, exports, revenue or FX supply**?
flow.notes: Sources: NBS GDP Q2 2026 (oil 4.16% of real GDP); NBS Foreign Trade in Goods Q2 2026 via Intelpoint (crude ₦12.91trn; non-crude ₦14.11trn; non-oil ₦3.72trn = 13.8% of total). Oil and gas share = (27.02 − 3.72) / 27.02 = 86.2%. In the 2000s oil supplied about 95% of FX earnings (LBS case IB-90).

flow.title: Small Words, Big Mistakes
steps: A **percentage point (pp)** is the simple difference between two rates.
A **percent change** is the change relative to the starting level.
Markets speak in **basis points**: 1 pp = 100 bp. The September 2026 MPC cut was **350 bp**.
'Food weight cut by over 22 per cent' (Feb 2025 headline) is right as a percent — the weight fell **11.8 points**.
flow.aside: A loan priced at 'MPR + 4%' fell from 30.5% to 27.0% after the September 2026 cut: a **3.5 pp** fall in the rate, which cuts the interest bill by **11.5%**. Both numbers are right; they answer different questions.
flow.result: Say **pp** for changes in rates. Mixing the two misstates a change by a factor of two to four.
flow.notes: Sources: CBN/NBS CPI (Dec 2024 34.80%, Sep 2026 14.63%); CBN MPC (MPR 26.5% → 23%, Sep 2026); The Guardian, Feb 2025, 'NBS unveils new inflation template, reduces food weight to 40%' (guardian.ng/news/nbs-unveils-new-inflation-template-reduces-food-weight-to-40/). Year-on-year vs month-on-month and base effects are in the appendix.

flow.title: Real vs Nominal: One Revenue Figure, Three Answers
points: **Real growth**: (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1 = 1.30 ÷ 1.332 − 1 ≈ **−2.4%**. Volume fell.
The shortcut 'nominal − inflation' gives −3.2%: fine for small rates, off at Nigerian rates.
The board was celebrating a business that shrank. Report **real, naira and dollar** figures side by side.
Targets and bonuses set in nominal naira **reward inflation, not performance**.
flow.notes: Uses 2024 average inflation (33.24%) and annual-average exchange rates (₦645.19, ₦1,478.97), World Bank WDI. Which deflator? The firm's own price index gives volume growth; the CPI gives the customers' purchasing-power view. Ask participants to redo this for their own firm before Session 2.

flow.title: Naira per Dollar: Rationing, Then a Reset
points: Until 2023 the CBN held an official rate; the **bureau-de-change** rate shows the market's price. The gap peaked at **71% (May 2016)**.
A premium signals **rationing** — Principle 6 at work — and an incentive to arbitrage (Principle 4).
June 2023 unification: the naira moved from about **₦460 to ₦750/$** within weeks, then past **₦1,500**.
Today: **₦1,347/$** (CBN, 4 Nov 2026). **Use the rate you actually transact at.**
flow.notes: Source: CBN statistics — official central rate (daily, averaged monthly) and BDC monthly average (CBN series ends April 2021). Latest: CBN central rate ₦1,347.30/$, 4 Nov 2026. Session 11 covers regimes, unification and the trilemma.

flow.title: Did Savers Beat Inflation? The Real Policy Rate
points: Real rate = (1 + policy rate) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1 — the same arithmetic as real revenue.
For most of 2016–2024 it was **negative**, falling below **−8%** in 2024: naira savings lost value, pushing savers into dollars, land and stock.
Today: MPR **23%**, inflation **14.6%** → real rate **+7.3%**. Holding naira now **pays**.
Part of the jump in January 2025 is the **new CPI** — measurement, not just policy.
flow.notes: Source: CBN statistics (MPR and headline CPI, monthly). Exact Fisher formula. Sep 2026: 1.23 / 1.1463 − 1 = 7.3%. Ask: which cash and inventory habits did your firm learn when real rates were negative — and which should change now?

flow.title: Four Reasons Two Series Move Together
flow.lead: Correlation tells you that two series **move together**. It does not tell you **why** — or which way the arrow points.
flow.leadFoot: Before acting on 'X drives Y', rule out all four.

points.t: Bank credit and inflation both jumped after the 2023 devaluation: the weaker naira **revalued dollar loans** and **raised import prices**.
Branches that spend more on marketing sell more — partly because budgets are **set as a share of last year's sales**.
Policy and price shocks work with lags. A same-month correlation can show **no link, or the wrong sign**.
Two trending series always look related. Short windows and data-mining produce **spurious** patterns — the Kuznets curve story in the appendix is the classic.

flow.notes: Then show the oil–reserves chart: an obvious causal channel with a modest and unstable correlation. Then the method slide: how to get at cause.

flow.title: Oil Earns Nigeria's Dollars — Yet Reserves Don't Simply Track It
points: The causal channel is clear: oil and gas earn most of the FX (Trap 3).
Yet the correlation is only **0.54** in the same month — and **0.17** a year later.
Why? Oil-backed loans and forward sales, CBN intervention, Eurobond and loan inflows, and **2026's reserve build despite** a volatile oil price.
A causal link can hide inside a weak correlation, and a strong correlation can hide no link at all.
flow.notes: Sources: CBN gross external reserves (month-end), FRED MCOILBRENTEU; correlations computed in s01_figures.py over Jan 2015 – Oct 2026. Brent averaged $123.9 in Oct 2026 (FRED) — a live issue for the dashboard in Part 3.

flow.title: Did Our Price Rise Cut Volumes? Use a Comparison Group
steps: **Naïve reading**: volumes fell 8% after a 10% price rise, so elasticity ≈ −0.8. Cut the price back?
But a fuel-price shock hit **both** cities. Abuja, with **no** price change, fell 5% anyway.
**Difference-in-differences**: the price rise explains only −8% − (−5%) = **−3%** → elasticity ≈ **−0.3**. Demand is fairly inelastic; keep the price.
Stronger designs: **randomised tests** (price a random half of outlets), and **natural experiments** (a policy that hits some regions or products and not others).
flow.aside: Ask of any 'X caused Y' claim: **compared with what?** Without a comparison group that faced the same shocks, you are measuring the shock, not your decision.
flow.result: Cause needs a **counterfactual**: what would have happened without the decision?
flow.notes: Illustrative numbers. The comparison works only if Lagos and Abuja would have moved alike without the price change ('parallel trends'). Link to Session 2 (elasticity) and Session 3 (forecasting). Mention that the economics of randomised experiments (Banerjee–Duflo–Kremer, Nobel 2019) and natural experiments (Card–Angrist–Imbens, Nobel 2021) are this same idea.

flow.q: A director says: 'Inflation fell from 34.8% in December 2024 to 24.5% in January 2025 — down 10% in a month. We can cut prices.' What is the best response?
options: The fall partly reflects the new CPI base and basket; January has since been revised to 27.6%, and it is a 10-point fall, not 10% — compare like with like before repricing
He is right: a 10-point fall in one month is strong evidence that price pressures have ended
He is right on the direction but wrong on size: it fell about 30%, so cut prices even more
Ignore inflation data altogether; watch only the exchange rate
flow.explain: A. Three corrections in one: a rebasing break, a later revision, and points vs percent. B ignores the measurement break; C computes the percent change correctly (−30%) but draws the wrong conclusion from a broken comparison; D throws away useful information.

flow.q: Which pair of signals would best tell an FMCG board, **this month**, that demand is weakening?

The CPI base year and the GDP base year
The 10-year bond yield and the oil price
The PMI new-orders index and the firm's own distributor orders and collections

flow.question: What else do I need to master Session 1 on my own?

flow.title: Economics Is the Study of Choice Under Scarcity
flow.lead: **Scarcity**: society has limited resources and cannot produce everything people want. **Economics** studies how society manages those scarce resources.
flow.leadFoot: A firm is a small society: limited cash, capacity, FX, management attention.

points.t: Scarce dollars to raw materials or to a dollar loan? More 50 cl or 1 litre packs? Economic questions before they are finance questions.
Customers trade off food against transport; competitors trade off price against margin; government trades off subsidies against capital spending.
**Microeconomics**: households and firms in markets (Sessions 2–5). **Macroeconomics**: economy-wide inflation, growth, interest and exchange rates (Sessions 6–12).

flow.title: The Circular-Flow Diagram: The Simplest Model of the Economy
points: A **model** is a simplified map: it leaves out detail on purpose so we can see how parts connect.
**Households** own labour, land and capital; **firms** hire them to produce goods and services.
Every naira one person spends is a naira of **income** for someone else: total spending = total income = **GDP**.
Left out on purpose: government, banks and the rest of the world (Sessions 7–11).
When households' real incomes fall, the flow into your goods market shrinks.

flow.kicker: TWO KINDS OF STATEMENT · MANKIW CH. 2
flow.title: Positive vs Normative: Scientist or Policy Adviser?

left.title: Positive statements
left.tag: Describe how the world is — testable
items: 'Removing the petrol subsidy raised transport fares.'
'A 10% depreciation raises the CPI by x% within a year.'
Settled with **evidence**.

right.title: Normative statements
right.tag: Prescribe how it should be — values
items: 'The CBN should cut rates to help manufacturers.'
'Nigeria ought to ban textile imports.'
Involve **values and priorities**, not only facts.

flow.note: Why economists disagree: different **scientific judgements**, different **values** — and less often than headlines suggest.

flow.title: Classify Each Statement
items: Inflation fell from 34.8% in December 2024 to 14.6% in September 2026.
Inflation of 15% is still far too high for Nigeria.
Higher minimum wages reduce formal-sector hiring of young workers.
The government should use oil windfalls to pay down debt rather than raise salaries.
Banks that raised capital in the recapitalisation have grown lending faster.
A strong naira is good for the country.
flow.note: Tip: **should, ought, too high, good, fair** usually signal a normative claim. A positive claim can be **false** and still be positive.
flow.notes: ANSWERS: 1 positive (true, but note the CPI break). 2 normative. 3 positive (testable; evidence is mixed). 4 normative. 5 positive (testable). 6 normative — good for whom? Importers and consumers gain; exporters and naira oil revenue lose.

flow.title: GDP: What Is Counted, and What Is Not
flow.lead:
GDP is the **market value** of all **final** goods and services **produced in a country** in a period.

**C** consumption · **I** investment · **G** government purchases (not transfers) · **NX** exports − imports
flow.leadFoot: Because spending = income, GDP also measures total income.

points.t: Valued at market prices so we can add rice and phone calls. Unpriced work — home care, subsistence — is largely left out.
Count the loaf, not the flour in it, or you double-count.
GDP counts output inside Nigeria, whoever owns the factory; GNI counts income of Nigerians wherever earned.
Q2 2026: nominal GDP **+18.4%**, real **+4.4%**. The gap (≈13.4%) is price change — the **GDP deflator**.

flow.notes: NBS GDP Q2 2026: nominal ₦119.29trn (basic prices), +18.43%; real +4.43%. Implied deflator 1.1843 / 1.0443 − 1 = 13.4%.

flow.kicker: WHY THE CPI IS IMPERFECT · MANKIW CH. 23
flow.title: Three Biases Every Price Index Carries

cards.title: Substitution bias
cards.body: When rice gets dearer, families switch to garri or yam. A fixed basket ignores the switch, so it **overstates** the rise in the cost of living.

cards.title: New goods
cards.body: Mobile money and ride-hailing widened choice and cut costs. A basket fixed in an old base year **misses them** until it is rebased.

cards.title: Unmeasured quality
cards.body: If a phone costs 20% more but does twice as much, part of the 'price rise' is really **more quality**.

flow.note: These biases are why statistics offices **rebase**. Rebasing reduces the bias — but breaks the series.

flow.title: Which Change Are You Looking At?
steps: **Year on year** compares with the same month last year: smooth, but it carries **twelve months of history**.
**Month on month** shows the latest momentum — noisy and seasonal (harvests, festive demand).
**Annualise** a monthly rate: (1 + m)¹² − 1. Core: 1.0111¹² − 1 ≈ **14.2%**.
Reading: headline momentum looks near zero because **food fell after the harvest**; underlying (core) pressure still runs at about 14% a year.
flow.aside: **Base effects**: if prices jumped in a month last year, the y/y rate falls mechanically when that month drops out — even if nothing improves today. The mid-2023 petrol-price jump did exactly this to mid-2024 readings.
flow.result: Ask: **compared with when? seasonally adjusted? headline or core?**
flow.notes: Source: NBS CPI September 2026 (headline 14.63% y/y, 0.06% m/m; food 19.59%, −1.55%; core 12.95%, 1.11%), as reported by the Gazette, 16 Oct 2026.

flow.title: The Kuznets Curve: A Big Theory Built on a Special Period
flow.lead: In 1955 Simon Kuznets suggested inequality **naturally falls** as economies develop. The idea spread worldwide.
flow.leadFoot: Kuznets himself warned the data were special; the warning was forgotten.

points.t: Kuznets built the first US income-distribution series from tax returns, **1913–1948**, and documented every method.
The fall in US inequality came largely from the **Great Depression and World War II**, not an automatic law.
Longer, wider data show inequality **rising again** in many countries from the 1980s.
A trend from a short or unusual window — say 2016–2020, or the post-2023 reform period — is a **hypothesis**, not a law.

flow.notes: Piketty (2014), Introduction: 'A Debate without Data?' and 'The Kuznets Curve: Good News in the Midst of the Cold War'.

flow.title: Nigeria's Unemployment Rate: 33% to 4% — by Definition
flow.lead: The headline unemployment rate went from **33.3% (Q4 2020)** to **4.1% (Q1 2023)**. Most of the fall is a **change of definition**, not of jobs.
flow.leadFoot: The two numbers are not comparable.

points.t: Under the new method, anyone who worked **at least one hour** for pay or profit in the past week counts as employed (the ILO standard).
Time-related underemployment — working under 40 hours and wanting more — was **12.2%** in Q1 2023.

points.h: Why it matters for the trade-off
points.t: With most jobs informal, tightening shows up first in **hours, incomes and informal sales**, not in the headline rate.
Track your own **footfall, basket size and distributor orders** as the real-time labour-income signal.

flow.notes: Source: NBS Labour Force Survey, new methodology (Q1 2023, 4.1%; underemployment 12.2%); old-methodology Q4 2020 rate 33.3% — TheCable, Aug 2023.

figures.title: What a Tonne of Imported Wheat Costs in Naira
points: Nigeria imports almost all its milling wheat: USDA puts imports at about 6.7 million tonnes in 2025/26 and forecasts 7.2 mt for 2026/27; under 1% of major millers' flour uses local grain.
So the naira cost of wheat = world price × exchange rate. Either can move it.
2022: the world price spiked (Russia–Ukraine). 2023–24: the naira did the damage. 2026: the world price is up about 46% since January — naira cost is back near its Feb 2024 peak.
Every flour-based business — bread, noodles, pasta, biscuits — faced this same shock.

figures.title: A Cost Shock Shifts Supply Up — the Price Rises by Less
points: Higher flour costs shift supply up: firms need more to supply the same quantity.
New equilibrium: price +10%, quantity −13% in this example.
The price rises by less than the cost: customers pay part, producers absorb part.
Steeper (less elastic) demand → more of the shock lands on customers.

figures.title: Prices Tripled — Volumes Did Not Collapse
points: Lagos shelf price went from about ₦162 to ₦518 a pack between 2022 and 2025.
Average weekly volumes 2022 → 2025: North +12%, Lagos −5%, South-East −9% — far smaller moves than prices.
Looks like customers do not care about price. Do not believe it yet.
Incomes, rivals' prices and the general price level all moved at the same time.

figures.title: Inflation Hides the Elasticity
points: Units against shelf price gives an elasticity of just −0.09 — 'price barely matters'.
But every price was rising: rivals' prices, wages, the whole price level.
Shoppers respond to our price relative to alternatives and to their income.
To see the true response, hold the other drivers constant — the Session 1 lesson on correlation.

figures.title: What Customers Really Respond To
points: Own price −1.47: a 1% rise in our price, all else equal, cuts volume by about 1.5%.
Cross price +0.73: a 1% rise in a rival's price lifts our volume by about 0.7% — close substitutes.
Income +1.11: as incomes rise, customers buy more.
Method: regress log(units) on log(own price), log(rival price), log(real income), a trend and region.

figures.title: When Does a Price Rise Raise Revenue?
points: Elasticity −0.5: a 20% price rise raises revenue.
At our −1.47, a 20% rise cuts revenue by about 8%.
Revenue is not profit: a rise that covers higher costs can still protect margin.
When all firms raise prices together, the relevant elasticity is smaller than one brand's.

figures.title: Big Jumps Hurt More Than the Arithmetic Says
points: Actual sales compared with the elasticity model's prediction.
Promotion weeks (price below usual) sold about 4% more than predicted.
Up to 5% above usual: no extra penalty. More than about 10% above: −7.7% (13 weeks — a small sample).
The penalty fades as the new price becomes the new normal.

figures.title: What a 15% Discount Buys
points: Promotion weeks (15% off) sold 32–36% more packs than normal weeks.
Part is new demand; part is pantry loading — buying earlier, not more.
Measure the weeks after a promotion: a dip means you borrowed from the future.
Frequent promotions reset reference prices downward.

figures.title: How Much of the Flour Shock to Pass On?
points: The shock adds ₦63 to a pack that sells for ₦500 and costs ₦350.
Absorb it all: volume holds; profit falls to 58% of its old level.
Pass it all on, rivals holding: volume −16%, profit 84%. If rivals follow: volume −8%, profit 92%.
Every miller pays the same world price × naira — rivals are likely to follow.

items: A cost shock is shared: the side that can least escape it bears more.
Separate a move along a curve from a shift of it — inflation hides the true elasticity.
Own, cross and income elasticities tell you how volume reacts to you, rivals and the economy.
Check revenue, profit and margin together; your margin implies an elasticity.
Customers judge prices against a reference price and by fairness: stagger, explain, resize.

hook.title: Flour Is Up 40%. What Do We Charge?
hook.quote: “Our flour bill has jumped 40%. Just add it to the price — everybody eats noodles.”

concepts.title: Own-Price Elasticity of Demand
concepts.plain: Elasticity is the % change in quantity for a 1% change in price. Bigger than 1 (ignoring the sign) = elastic: customers react strongly. Smaller than 1 = inelastic.
concepts.formula: elasticity = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price
concepts.example: Our noodles (stylised data): −1.47. A 10% price rise, rivals holding, loses about 13% of volume.
concepts.why: Elastic demand: a price rise cuts revenue. Inelastic demand: a price rise raises revenue. Knowing which you face is the start of every pricing decision.

concepts.title: Reference Prices and Loss Aversion
concepts.plain: Shoppers judge a price against the price they are used to — their reference price. Paying more than usual feels like a loss, and people weigh losses about twice as heavily as equal gains (Kahneman & Tversky).
concepts.formula: pain of a ₦50 rise  >  pleasure of a ₦50 cut
concepts.example: In our data, weeks priced more than 10% above the usual price sold about 7.7% fewer packs than the elasticity alone predicts.
concepts.why: Several small, explained increases usually cost less volume than one big jump. Pack-size changes, clear communication and timing all manage the reference price.

checks.q: A competitor cuts its noodle price by 10%. Our cross-price elasticity is +0.73. Holding our price, what happens to our volume?
options: Rises about 7% — their cut expands the whole market
Falls about 15% — use the own-price elasticity
Falls about 7% — some of our customers switch to them
No change — cross-price elasticity applies only to complements

flow.title: Flour Is Up 40%. What Do We Charge?
flow.quote: “Our flour bill has jumped 40%. Just add it to the price — everybody eats noodles.”
flow.intro: Before signing the new price list, a good manager asks three questions — the three parts of today:

points.title: 1 · Who bears the cost?
points.body: A cost shock is shared between buyers and sellers. The split depends on how each side responds.

points.title: 2 · How sensitive are buyers?
points.body: If a 10% price rise loses 15% of volume, 'just pass it on' shrinks revenue.

points.title: 3 · What price feels fair?
points.body: Shoppers compare with the price they are used to. Big jumps hurt more than the arithmetic says.

flow.notes:
Ask three or four participants to commit to a pass-through percentage now (0%, 50%, 100%?). Write the numbers on the board and revisit them at the end.

The noodles maker is a teaching case built on stylised data; the wheat-cost chart on the next slide is real.

flow.title: What a Tonne of Imported Wheat Costs in Naira
points: Nigeria imports almost all its milling wheat: USDA puts imports at about **6.7 million tonnes** in 2025/26 and forecasts **7.2 mt** for 2026/27; under **1%** of major millers' flour uses local grain.
So the naira cost of wheat = **world price × exchange rate**. Either can move it.
2022: the **world price** spiked (Russia–Ukraine). 2023–24: the **naira** did the damage. 2026: the world price is up about **46%** since January — naira cost is back near its Feb 2024 peak.
Every flour-based business — bread, noodles, pasta, biscuits — faced this same shock.
flow.notes: Sources: FRED PWHEAMTUSDM (IMF global price of wheat, US$/tonne, monthly) × CBN official central rate (monthly average); computed in s02_figures.py: ₦35.7k/t (Jan 2015) → ₦330.1k (Feb 2024 peak) → ₦327.5k (Sep 2026); world price $169/t (Jan 2026) → $247/t (Sep 2026). USDA FAS via Milling Middle East & Africa, 29 Sep 2025 (2025/26 imports 6.7 mt, up from 6.25 mt; less than one percent of major millers' flour contains domestic wheat) and 6 Mar 2026 (USDA Grain & Feed Annual: 2026/27 imports forecast at 7.2 mt). This is a world benchmark price, not the landed cost in Lagos (add freight, insurance, duties and port charges).

flow.label: PART
flow.title: Who Bears a Cost Shock?
flow.sub: Demand, supply and the split of a price rise.
flow.question: When costs rise, how much ends up in the price — and how much in our margin?

flow.kicker: THE TWO SIDES OF A MARKET · MANKIW CH. 4
flow.title: What Moves Demand, and What Moves Supply

left.title: Demand: willingness to buy
left.tag: Slopes down — higher price, fewer packs
items: Own price: a move **along** the curve
Income, prices of substitutes and complements
Tastes, population, expectations of future prices
These **shift** the whole curve

right.title: Supply: willingness to sell
right.tag: Slopes up — higher price, more packs
items: Own price: a move **along** the curve
Input costs: wheat, diesel, packaging, the naira
Technology, number of sellers, taxes and levies
These **shift** the whole curve

flow.note: A change in **price** moves you **along** a curve. A change in **anything else** **shifts** the curve. Most pricing mistakes come from mixing the two.

flow.title: Solve the Market Before and After the Shock
steps: **Equilibrium**: set demand = supply. 1,000 − 2P = −200 + 2P → P = **₦300**, Q = **400**.
A ₦60 cost rise means firms need ₦60 more to supply each quantity: supply shifts **up by ₦60**.
Buyers pay **₦30** of the ₦60; sellers' net price falls by the other **₦30** (from ₦300 to ₦270). Lost volume is an extra cost on top.
flow.aside: **Pass-through rule** for straight-line curves: share passed to price = supply responsiveness ÷ (supply + demand responsiveness) = 2 ÷ (2 + 2) = **50%**. The **less** price-sensitive the buyers, the **more** they pay.
flow.result: A cost shock is **shared**. Who pays more depends on who can **walk away** more easily.
flow.notes: Mankiw ch. 4 (equilibrium) and ch. 6 (tax incidence) use the same logic: a per-unit cost or tax is split by relative elasticities, not by who writes the cheque. With demand Q = 1,000 − 2P the slope term is 2 for both curves, hence 50%.

flow.title: A Cost Shock Shifts Supply Up — the Price Rises by Less
points: Higher flour costs shift supply **up**: firms need more to supply the same quantity.
New equilibrium: price **+10%**, quantity **−13%** in this example.
The price rises by **less than the cost**: customers pay part, producers absorb part.
Steeper (less elastic) demand → more of the shock lands on customers.
flow.notes: In the diagram the cost shift is 90 and the price rises by about 50: roughly 56% pass-through.

flow.title: Nigerian Shocks, Read as Demand and Supply

cards.title: Petrol subsidy removal (2023)
cards.body: A supply shock to everything that moves. NBS: average intra-city bus fare rose from **₦650 to ₦1,285** — **+98% in one month** (May → June 2023).

cards.title: Naira depreciation (2023–24)
cards.body: Imported wheat, packaging and machinery cost more naira: supply shifts **up** across manufacturing — see the wheat chart.

cards.title: Falling real incomes
cards.body: When wages lag inflation, demand for non-essentials shifts **down**; shoppers **trade down** to smaller packs and cheaper brands.

cards.title: New sellers online
cards.body: Social-media and e-commerce sellers add supply and make prices easier to compare: each seller's demand becomes **more elastic**.

flow.notes: Source: NBS Transport Fare Watch, June 2023 (intra-city bus fare per drop ₦649.59 → ₦1,285.41, +97.88% m/m; inter-city ₦4,002.16 → ₦5,686.49, +42.09%), reported by Nairametrics, 14 Aug 2023. Inference for discussion (not measured by NBS): fares could nearly double because commuters had few short-run alternatives — inelastic demand allows high pass-through.

flow.kicker: GOVERNMENT IN THE MARKET · MANKIW CH. 6
flow.title: Taxes, Ceilings and Floors: Who Really Pays?
flow.lead: The burden of a tax or a cost falls on whichever side **can least escape it** — regardless of who hands the money to the government.
flow.leadFoot: Policy names the payer; elasticity decides the bearer.

points.t: Nigeria kept VAT at **7.5%** in the 2025 reforms. From **1 January 2026** basic food moved from **exempt** to **zero-rated**: sellers can now reclaim the VAT on their inputs. Shoppers gain only if that cost saving is passed on — likelier where competition is strong.

Holding petrol at about **₦185–₦199/litre** (NNPC pump prices) until end-May 2023 and the naira below its market rate produced **queues, rationing and parallel markets** — the price was paid another way.
A minimum price above equilibrium leaves sellers with **unsold supply** — the logic behind debates on minimum wages and guaranteed farm prices.
When a tax, levy or subsidy changes, estimate **your** share using elasticities — not the headline rate.

flow.notes: Sources: Forvis Mazars, 'VAT & Nigeria 2025 Tax Reforms' (7.5% retained; basic food zero-rated; effective 1 January 2026). Basic food was already VAT-exempt under the old VAT Act, so the change is about input VAT, not a 7.5% cut at the till; check whether a product such as noodles counts as basic food. Mankiw ch. 6 ('Supply, Demand and Government Policies'). Zero-rating, unlike exemption, lets suppliers reclaim input VAT. Petrol: NNPC pump prices were about ₦184–₦199 by region before 31 May 2023, raised to ₦488–₦557 (ThisDay, 31 May 2023).

flow.label: PART
flow.title: Elasticity: How Much Do Customers React?
flow.sub: One number that should sit beside every price decision.
flow.question: If we raise the price, how many customers do we lose — and does revenue rise or fall?

flow.title: Own-Price Elasticity of Demand
flow.plain: Elasticity is the **% change in quantity for a 1% change in price**. Bigger than 1 (ignoring the sign) = **elastic**: customers react strongly. Smaller than 1 = **inelastic**.
flow.formula: elasticity = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price
flow.example: Our noodles (stylised data): **−1.47**. A 10% price rise, rivals holding, loses about **13%** of volume.
flow.why: Elastic demand: a price rise **cuts revenue**. Inelastic demand: a price rise **raises revenue**. Knowing which you face is the start of every pricing decision.

flow.title: Elasticity and the Revenue Test, Step by Step
steps: Use the **midpoint** method so the answer is the same up or down: %ΔP = 50 ÷ 525 = **9.5%**; %ΔQ = −13,000 ÷ 93,500 = **−13.9%**.
Elasticity = −13.9 ÷ 9.5 = **−1.46**: elastic.
**Revenue test**: price up, revenue down (₦50.0m → ₦47.85m) — the signature of elastic demand.
But **profit** is a different question: with a ₦350 unit cost, margin per week goes from ₦15.0m to **₦17.4m**. Fewer packs, more profit.
flow.result: Elasticity tells you what happens to **revenue**; add costs to see what happens to **profit**.
flow.notes: Profit: (500 − 350) × 100,000 = ₦15.0m; (550 − 350) × 87,000 = ₦17.4m. This is why 'we'll lose volume' is not by itself an argument against a price rise.

flow.title: Why Some Customers Shrug and Others Walk Away
flow.lead: Demand is more elastic when customers have **close substitutes**, the item is a **luxury** or a **big share of the budget**, and they have **time** to adjust.
flow.leadFoot: And the narrower the market you define, the more elastic it is.

points.t: One noodle brand among many → elastic. All noodles together → much less so.
Commuters in June 2023 still had to get to work: intra-city fares nearly **doubled** in a month, yet transport operators could make them stick.
A ₦50 rise on a ₦500 pack matters more to a low-income family spending most of its income on food.
Short run: few options. Long run: households switch fuel, car-pool, buy in bulk, change brands — elasticity **rises**.

flow.notes: Mankiw ch. 5. The brand-versus-market distinction drives the pass-through decision at the end of the session.

flow.title: Prices Tripled — Volumes Did Not Collapse
points: Lagos shelf price went from about **₦162 to ₦518** a pack between 2022 and 2025.
Average weekly volumes 2022 → 2025: North **+12%**, Lagos **−5%**, South-East **−9%** — far smaller moves than prices.
Looks like customers do not care about price. **Do not believe it yet.**
Incomes, rivals' prices and the general price level all moved at the same time.

flow.title: Inflation Hides the Elasticity
points: Units against shelf price gives an elasticity of just **−0.09** — 'price barely matters'.
But **every** price was rising: rivals' prices, wages, the whole price level.
Shoppers respond to our price **relative** to alternatives and to their income.
To see the true response, **hold the other drivers constant** — the Session 1 lesson on correlation.
flow.notes: Same confusion as moving along a curve versus shifting it: over 2022–2025 demand was shifting while we moved along it.

flow.title: What Customers Really Respond To
points: **Own price −1.47**: a 1% rise in our price, all else equal, cuts volume by about 1.5%.
**Cross price +0.73**: a 1% rise in a rival's price lifts our volume by about 0.7% — close substitutes.
**Income +1.11**: as incomes rise, customers buy more.
Method: regress log(units) on log(own price), log(rival price), log(real income), a trend and region.
flow.notes: Income and the time trend move together, so the income elasticity is less precise. Treat it as 'about one'. No separate promotion dummy: in these data promotions work through the price cut, so a dummy would soak up price variation and bias the elasticity towards zero (it gives about −1.15; the data were generated with a true own-price elasticity of −1.4). The lab lets participants try both.

flow.title: Three Elasticities Every Manager Should Know
head: Elasticity
Question it answers
Our estimate
Business use
rows: If we raise our price 1%, what happens to our volume?
If a rival raises its price 1%, what happens to our volume?
Is the rival a close substitute? Will they follow?
If customers' real income rises 1%, what happens to our volume?
If the market price rises 1%, how much more will sellers offer?
Who bears a cost shock; capacity planning
flow.note: Cross-price **positive** = substitutes (rival noodles). **Negative** = complements (noodles and seasoning). Income elasticity **negative** = an inferior good that people buy less of as they get richer.

flow.title: When Does a Price Rise Raise Revenue?
points: Elasticity −0.5: a 20% price rise **raises** revenue.
At our −1.47, a 20% rise **cuts** revenue by about **8%**.
Revenue is not profit: a rise that covers higher costs can still protect margin.
When **all** firms raise prices together, the relevant elasticity is smaller than one brand's.

flow.title: Your Gross Margin Reveals the Elasticity You Assume
steps: The **markup rule** (Lerner): at the profit-maximising price, (price − marginal cost) ÷ price = 1 ÷ |elasticity|.
Our margin is (500 − 350) ÷ 500 = **30%**, which is optimal only if |e| ≈ **3.3**.
Our measured short-run brand elasticity is **1.47**. Either we are **under-pricing**, or the true long-run elasticity is higher (rivals react, entry, trading down).
Useful test before any repricing: **which elasticity are we implicitly assuming?**
flow.result: Margins and elasticities must be **consistent**. If they are not, one of them is wrong.
flow.notes: Lerner index; derivation in any managerial-economics text (e.g. Baye & Prince, course reading list). The rule assumes the firm sets price with demand of constant elasticity and holds rivals' prices fixed. Strictly the rule needs **marginal** cost; the ₦350 average unit cost stands in for it here. Use it as a consistency check, not a pricing formula.

flow.q: A competitor cuts its noodle price by 10%. Our cross-price elasticity is +0.73. Holding our price, what happens to our volume?
options: Rises about 7% — their cut expands the whole market
Falls about 15% — use the own-price elasticity
Falls about 7% — some of our customers switch to them
No change — cross-price elasticity applies only to complements
flow.explain: C. A cross-price elasticity of +0.73 means our volume moves 0.73% in the **same** direction as the rival's price. A 10% cut by them → about 7% fewer packs for us. A gets the sign wrong; B uses the wrong elasticity; D has substitutes and complements reversed.

flow.label: PART
flow.title: Behaviour, Promotions and the Decision
flow.sub: Customers are not calculators.
flow.question: How much of the flour shock should we pass on — how fast, and in what form?

flow.title: Reference Prices and Loss Aversion
flow.plain: Shoppers judge a price against the price they are **used to** — their **reference price**. Paying more than usual feels like a **loss**, and people weigh losses about **twice** as heavily as equal gains (Kahneman & Tversky).
flow.formula: pain of a ₦50 rise  >  pleasure of a ₦50 cut
flow.example: In our data, weeks priced **more than 10% above** the usual price sold about **7.7%** fewer packs than the elasticity alone predicts.
flow.why: Several small, explained increases usually cost less volume than one big jump. Pack-size changes, clear communication and timing all manage the reference price.
flow.notes: Kahneman & Tversky, 'Prospect Theory' (Econometrica, 1979); Tversky & Kahneman (1992) estimate a loss-aversion coefficient of about 2.25. The 7.7% penalty is from the stylised dataset.

flow.title: Big Jumps Hurt More Than the Arithmetic Says
points: Actual sales compared with the elasticity model's prediction.
Promotion weeks (price **below** usual) sold about **4%** more than predicted.
Up to 5% above usual: no extra penalty. **More than about 10% above: −7.7%** (13 weeks — a small sample).
The penalty fades as the new price becomes the new normal.
flow.notes: Reference price modelled as a moving average of past shelf prices (each week: 80% of the previous reference plus 20% of last week's shelf price): a teaching approximation of how shoppers' memories adjust.

flow.title: Customers Punish Prices That Feel Unfair
flow.lead: A hardware store raises the price of snow shovels from **$15 to $20** the morning after a snowstorm. **82%** of respondents called it **unfair**.
flow.leadFoot: Raising prices because **costs** rose is accepted far more readily than raising them because **demand** rose.

points.t: Explaining a rise by a visible cost (wheat, diesel, the naira) protects goodwill. That is today's case.
Surge pricing on ride-hailing apps in rain or rush hour balances riders and drivers — but customers resent it.
Algorithms can price by product, store, hour and customer. Personalised prices that customers would object to invite **backlash and regulators**.
Be transparent about costs; cap surges on essentials; never personalise in ways you could not defend in public.

flow.notes: Kahneman, Knetsch & Thaler, 'Fairness as a Constraint on Profit Seeking: Entitlements in the Market', American Economic Review 76(4), 1986. Thaler's 'Misbehaving' (2015) retells the study. Session 4 returns to data, platforms and pricing power.

flow.title: What a 15% Discount Buys
points: Promotion weeks (15% off) sold **32–36%** more packs than normal weeks.
Part is new demand; part is **pantry loading** — buying earlier, not more.
Measure the weeks **after** a promotion: a dip means you borrowed from the future.
Frequent promotions reset reference prices **downward**.

flow.title: A 15% Discount Needs Volume to Double — We Got +34%
steps: A 15% discount (₦75) **halves** the margin per pack, from ₦150 to ₦75.
To earn the same margin, volume must rise by 150 ÷ 75 − 1 = **100%**.
Our promotions lifted volume by about **34%**, so each promotion week cost about **₦5m** of margin.
A promotion pays only if it wins **lasting new customers** or clears stock that would otherwise be lost — measure that, not the week's volume.
flow.result: Required uplift = margin ÷ (margin − discount) − 1. With thin margins, small discounts need **huge** volume gains.
flow.notes: Margin arithmetic: 100,000 × 150 = ₦15.0m; 134,000 × 75 = ₦10.05m. The 34% uplift is the Lagos figure from the stylised data.

flow.title: How Much of the Flour Shock to Pass On?
points: The shock adds **₦63** to a pack that sells for ₦500 and costs ₦350.
**Absorb it all**: volume holds; profit falls to **58%** of its old level.
**Pass it all on**, rivals holding: volume −16%, profit **84%**. If rivals follow: volume −8%, profit **92%**.
Every miller pays the same world price × naira — rivals are **likely to follow**.
flow.notes: Constant-elasticity model: own −1.47; own + cross ≈ −0.74 when rivals follow. ₦500 and ₦350 are stylised.

flow.title: How to Pass On a Cost Shock Without Breaking the Brand

cards.title: Stagger and signal
cards.body: Two or three steps rather than one jump; announce the **cost reason** (wheat, naira) — the fairness effect works for you.

cards.title: Resize and re-mix
cards.body: Smaller packs at familiar price points protect the **reference price**; premium variants carry more of the increase.

cards.title: Take cost out
cards.body: Recipe, packaging, logistics and procurement savings reduce the share you need to pass on at all.

flow.note: Watch three numbers weekly after a price change: **volume vs forecast, rivals' prices and distributor stock** — and be ready to adjust the next step.
flow.notes: Pack-size changes ('shrinkflation') manage reference prices but can damage trust if hidden; disclose clearly. Session 3 shows how to forecast the volume response.

flow.q: Flour costs rise 40% for every noodles maker in Nigeria. Which recommendation is best supported by today's analysis?
options: Rivals face the same shock and will likely follow, so pass on most of the cost — in steps, explained by the cost reason
Absorb the cost: any price rise hands customers to rivals
Raise prices by exactly 40%, since flour rose 40%
Price barely matters — our data show an elasticity near zero
flow.explain: A. When all firms face the same cost they tend to move together, so the volume loss is smaller (own + cross ≈ −0.74), and cost-based increases are judged fair. B ignores rivals' costs; C confuses the flour rise with the unit-cost rise (flour is 45% of cost); D is the inflation trap.

flow.title: Lab 2: How Price-Sensitive Are Our Customers?
steps: Plot prices and volumes by region, 2022–2025.
Estimate the **naive elasticity** (units on price only) and explain why it misleads.
Estimate own-price, cross-price and income elasticities **holding other things constant**.
Check the **Lerner rule**: which elasticity does today's margin imply?
Test pass-through of 0%, 50% and 100% of the flour shock — with rivals holding and following.
flow.deliver: a three-sentence pricing recommendation to the MD: how much to pass on, how fast, and what to watch.

items: A cost shock is **shared**: the side that can least escape it bears more.
Separate a **move along** a curve from a **shift** of it — inflation hides the true elasticity.
**Own, cross and income** elasticities tell you how volume reacts to you, rivals and the economy.
Check **revenue, profit and margin** together; your margin implies an elasticity.
Customers judge prices against a **reference price** and by **fairness**: stagger, explain, resize.

flow.title: Why Sellers Respond Slowly — and Why It Matters
flow.lead: Supply elasticity = % change in quantity supplied for a 1% change in price. It is **low in the short run** (fixed capacity, contracts, imports in transit) and **higher in the long run**.
flow.leadFoot: Inelastic supply + a demand surge = a price spike.

points.t: Planting decisions are made a season ahead: food prices spike when a harvest disappoints, then ease.
FX shortages make supply of imported goods **very inelastic** — prices jump when demand rises.
When rivals are at full capacity, they cannot steal your customers — you can pass on more.

flow.title: Four Effects Every Pricing Manager Meets

cards.title: Anchoring
cards.body: The first number seen shapes what feels reasonable: show the premium pack first, and the standard pack feels cheap.

cards.title: Charm and round prices
cards.body: ₦499 reads as 'four hundred and something'; round prices signal quality. Test both.

cards.title: The decoy
cards.body: Adding an obviously inferior option makes a target option look better value.

cards.title: Pain of paying
cards.body: Mobile money and cards reduce the felt cost of paying; cash makes spending more painful.

flow.title: Common Pricing Mistakes

items.bad: “Volumes rose while prices rose, so demand is not price-sensitive.”
items.good: Hold **inflation, rivals' prices and income** constant first.

items.bad: Using one elasticity for every situation.
items.good: Distinguish **our brand alone** (more elastic) from **the whole market** (less elastic).

items.bad: Judging a price rise by revenue.
items.good: Judge it by **profit** and market position.

items.bad: Passing on a big cost increase in one jump.
items.good: Stagger, explain the cost reason, manage the **reference price**.

items.bad: Judging a promotion by the weeks it ran.
items.good: Count the **dip afterwards** and the margin given away.

items.bad: Assuming whoever pays a tax bears it.
items.good: Incidence follows **elasticities**, not the law.

figures.title: Fourteen Years of Cement Demand
points: Consumption grew from 18.7 Mt in 2012 to 32.2 Mt in 2025 — about 4.3% a year.
The 12-month moving average strips out the seasons and shows the trend.
Three shocks: the 2016 recession, the 2020 lockdown and the 2024 price spike.
Each time, demand returned to trend within about a year.

figures.title: The Rainy-Season Rhythm
points: February is about 14% above an average month; July and August about 18% below.
Rain stops site work, so demand dips from June to September.
Plan capacity, stock and cash for the peak months, not the annual average.
Schedule maintenance for the rainy season, when demand is lowest.

figures.title: Pretend It Is January 2024
points: Fit each method on 2012–2023 only and forecast 2024–2025.

flow.title: Read the Pattern
flow.sub: Trend, season, shock.

flow.title: Every Demand Series Has Three Parts

cards.title: Trend
cards.body: The long-run direction: population, urbanisation, incomes. Cement: about **4.3%** a year since 2012 in our series.

cards.title: Seasonality
cards.body: The pattern that repeats every year: the rainy season slows building from June to September.

cards.title: Shocks and noise
cards.body: Recessions, lockdowns, price spikes — and random month-to-month wobble no model can predict.

flow.note: Forecasting = project the **trend**, apply the **season**, and put a **range** around it for the shocks.

flow.title: Fourteen Years of Cement Demand
points: Consumption grew from **18.7 Mt** in 2012 to **32.2 Mt** in 2025 — about **4.3% a year**.
The 12-month moving average strips out the seasons and shows the **trend**.
Three shocks: the 2016 recession, the 2020 lockdown and the 2024 price spike.
Each time, demand returned to trend within about a year.

flow.title: The Rainy-Season Rhythm
points: February is about **14% above** an average month; July and August about **18% below**.
Rain stops site work, so demand dips from June to September.
Plan **capacity, stock and cash** for the peak months, not the annual average.
Schedule maintenance for the **rainy season**, when demand is lowest.

flow.title: Was August 2025 a Collapse?
steps: Raw numbers say August sales were **27% below** February. The sales director wants to cut production.
Divide each month by its **seasonal index** (how far that calendar month normally sits from average).
Seasonally adjusted, August was **1.4% above** February: the business is steady; only the weather changed.
Multiply by 12 to read any month as an **annual rate** — comparable with the full-year forecast.
flow.result: Never judge a month against the previous month without **seasonal adjustment**.
flow.notes: Seasonal index = the month effects from the trend × season regression, rescaled so the 12 months average 1.00 (s03_figures.py). The lab uses a simpler version — each month divided by its calendar-year average — which gives almost the same numbers (Feb 1.13, Aug 0.82). Official statistics do the same: compare NBS releases that are 'seasonally adjusted' with those that are not.

flow.title: Trend × Season: A Forecast in One Line
flow.plain: Next month's demand = the **trend level** for that month × the **seasonal index** for that calendar month. Both are fitted from history in one regression.
flow.example: Trend level for August 2026 ≈ 2.76 Mt; August index ≈ 0.82 → forecast ≈ **2.26 Mt**.
flow.why: Simple models are **transparent**: a manager can see and challenge every assumption. That matters more than an extra decimal of accuracy.
flow.notes: Technically: log(demand) = a + b·t + month dummies. The slope b gives growth of about 0.35% a month, 4.3% a year.

flow.title: Forecast Honestly
flow.sub: Test it, give a range, plan for scenarios.
flow.question: Which method should we trust — and how wrong could it be?

flow.title: Pretend It Is January 2024
points: Fit each method on **2012–2023 only** and forecast 2024–2025.
Then compare with what actually happened.
This **backtest** is the only honest way to judge a forecasting method.
The model followed both season and trend; 'same month last year' missed the growth.

flow.title: MAPE: How Far Off Were We, on Average?
steps: **Error** = forecast − actual. Over- and under-forecasts would cancel out, so take the **absolute** value.
Divide by the actual to compare months of different size, then average: **MAPE = 6.0%**.
Also check **% bias**: the average signed percentage error. A forecast that is always high is a planning problem even if MAPE looks fine.
Compare every method's MAPE on the **same backtest period**.
flow.result: MAPE answers 'how far off, on average?'; bias answers 'which way do we lean?' — track both.
flow.notes: Illustrative numbers. MAPE misbehaves when actuals are near zero (new products, intermittent demand); there, use mean absolute error or scaled errors (MASE).

flow.title: Which Method Forecast Best?
points: **Trend + seasonal model: 4.1%** average error — the best.
'Same month last year': **5.8%**. The budget rule 'last year + 5%': **6.6%**.
A flat average ignores the seasons: **10.9%**.
The 2024 price spike hurt every method — no method saw it coming. Hence ranges and scenarios.

flow.title: Simple, Combined and Humble Forecasts Win
flow.lead: In large forecasting competitions, **simple methods and combinations** of methods beat most complex ones — and people are reliably **over-confident**.
flow.leadFoot: Build the habit: backtest, combine, give a range.

points.t: 100,000 real time series. **12 of the 17** most accurate methods were **combinations**; the winner was a statistics–ML **hybrid**; all six **pure** machine-learning entries did **worse** than a simple combination benchmark.
Kahneman and Tversky: people build forecasts from the inside view of their own plan and ignore how similar plans turned out — so they are **systematically optimistic**.
Flyvbjerg's fix: start from the **track record of similar projects** (cost overruns, demand shortfalls) and adjust from there.
Ask of every forecast: **what is the base rate?** How did the last five capacity expansions in this industry actually fill?

flow.notes: Makridakis, Spiliotis & Assimakopoulos, 'The M4 Competition: Results, findings, conclusion and way forward', International Journal of Forecasting 34(4):802–808, 2018 (winner: Smyl's hybrid exponential-smoothing/RNN). The term 'inside view' comes from Kahneman & Lovallo (1993). Kahneman & Tversky (1979) on the planning fallacy; Flyvbjerg (2006), 'From Nobel Prize to project management: getting risks right', Project Management Journal. Tetlock & Gardner, 'Superforecasting' (2015), on calibration.

flow.title: Size the Market and Decide
flow.sub: Two routes to one number — then a capacity choice.
flow.question: Does the market add up — and how much capacity should we plan for?

flow.title: Start From the Whole Economy
steps: Top-down sizing starts from a **big, known number** and multiplies by a **rate of use**.
237.5m people × 0.129 t = **30.6 Mt**, about 10% below the industry's **33.9 Mt**. Yet 33.9 Mt ÷ 237.5m = **143 kg** — the source's own two numbers disagree.
Benchmark the rate: the world average is about **550 kg** a person. Nigeria uses a quarter of that — room to grow, or a sign of high prices and low incomes?
The **rate of use** carries all the weight — test it against peers at similar incomes.
flow.result: Top-down is fast; its weak point is the **use-per-person** rate — and even published sources can disagree with themselves.
flow.notes: Sources: World Bank SP.POP.TOTL (Nigeria 2025: 237,527,782). CemNet, 'Nigeria is in the middle of a new cement capacity frenzy' (30 Apr 2026): consumption about 33.9 Mt (+8.5%, citing Global Cement Report 16); 129 kg per capita and world average about 550 kg are CemNet's estimates. CemNet uses the same population, so its 129 kg and 33.9 Mt are mutually inconsistent (33.9 Mt implies 143 kg): probably different reference years. A good classroom exercise: spot the inconsistency before trusting either number.

flow.title: Add Up the Uses
flow.plain: **Bottom-up** sizing builds the market from its parts: homes, roads, factories and repairs, times the cement each needs.
flow.formula: market = Σ (units of activity × cement per unit)
flow.example: About 450,000 new homes × ~32 t = **14.4 Mt**, plus repairs (6.5), public works (6.0), commercial (4.5), precast (2.4) = **33.8 Mt**.
flow.why: Slower, but it shows **which segments drive demand** — and which ones a housing programme, a capital-budget release or a price shock would hit.
flow.notes: Segment assumptions are stylised teaching numbers. Real sizing would use NBS housing data, the federal capital budget, company reports and project pipelines.

flow.title: Do the Routes Agree?
points: Top-down **30.6 Mt**, bottom-up **33.8 Mt** (stylised), industry report **33.9 Mt**: within about 10%.

New homes are the biggest segment: watch **mortgage rates, real incomes and land policy**.
Three views pointing the same way — and an explanation for the gap — is what a board should see.

flow.title: How Much to Build? Weigh the Cost of Being Wrong

head: Per tonne of demand
₦ thousand
rows: Too little capacity: margin lost on a sale we cannot make
Too much capacity: cost of an idle tonne of capacity
total: Plan for the 71st percentile of demand

steps: A forecast is a **distribution**, not a number. Here: centre **32.9 Mt**, typical annual error about **3.5%**.
Ask what each error **costs**. Missing a sale loses ₦20k of margin; an idle tonne of capacity costs ₦8k.
When shortfalls cost more than surpluses, plan **above** the central forecast — at the **71st percentile**: about **33.6 Mt**.
If idle capacity were the dearer mistake, you would plan **below** the centre. The forecast is the same; the **decision** differs.
flow.result: Capacity = the demand level where the **cost of too little** balances the **cost of too much**.
flow.notes: The 'newsvendor' critical-fractile rule from operations management: choose the quantity at percentile Cu ÷ (Cu + Co). Here 20 ÷ 28 = 0.714; z = 0.57; 32.9 × exp(0.57 × 0.035) ≈ 33.6 Mt. With Nigeria's cement capacity already about double consumption, the cost of idle capacity for the industry is high — a reason to doubt the '5% and build' hook.

figures.title: Highly Concentrated — and More So Since 2024
points: From 2019 to 2023 MTN held 37–40% of active lines; the HHI stayed around 3,000 — already highly concentrated.

figures.title: Mobile Money: Kenya Tipped Early; Nigeria Is Catching Up Fast

concepts.title: The HHI: One Number for How Concentrated a Market Is
concepts.plain: Square each firm's market share (in %), then add them up. Ten equal firms give 1,000; five give 2,000; a monopoly gives 10,000.

concepts.title: A Platform Serves Two Groups Who Need Each Other
